en: I bow to the Lord of the Universe, whose power is inconceivable as the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution; who knows all things, possesses infinite forms, is liberated from all bonds, is a shoreless ocean of bliss, the beloved of Śrī, and a mass of pure consciousness. 1.
I bow perpetually at the lotus feet of Him, by whose grace I am indeed Viṣṇu and by whom everything is conceived within me; thus do I always know that which is the nature of the True Self. 2.
Someone, scorched by the sun of the threefold suffering and with a distressed mind,
being endowed with the means such as tranquility and so forth, inquires of a true guru.
O Blessed One, out of compassion, please tell me in brief that singular means by which I may be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence without effort. 4.
"Your manner of speaking appears excellent; I shall tell you.
Listen attentively and with a focused mind to this very point, clearly explained. (5)
That knowledge which arises from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and has as its object the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self— this alone is the means to liberation.
What is the individual soul (jīva), and what is the supreme self (para-ātman)? Or how could there be identity between the two?
And how could a statement such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) convey that [identity]? || 7 ||
To this we offer the resolution: who else is the living soul (jīva) but you yourself?
For you, who ask me "Who am I?", are none other than Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
"O Blessed One, even now I do not clearly know the meaning of the word itself;
tell me, how can I comprehend the sentence-meaning 'I am Brahman'? (9)
"You have spoken the truth; there is indeed no contradiction here.
For in this context, the comprehension of the meanings of individual words is the cause for the understanding of the meaning of the sentence. (10)
The witness of the internal organ and its modifications, whose form is consciousness, whose nature is bliss, and who is truth—that very Self, O Ka, do you not realize? 11.

Having abandoned the notion of the intellect directed toward the body and other such things, one should constantly contemplate, as one's own self, that which is of the nature of truth and bliss, the witness of the intellect, and the embodiment of knowledge. 12.
Because it possesses form and other qualities, the aggregate is therefore not the self, just like a jar;
and because it is a transformation of the great elements such as space, it is like a pot. (13)
If this aggregate is considered to be non-self by the force of the reasons already stated, then demonstrate the self directly, as one perceives a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. 14.
Just as the observer of a jar is in every way distinct from the jar, so too the observer of the body is not the body; determine this for yourself: "I am not [the body]. 15.
Thus, O seer of the senses, determine: "I am not the senses. Likewise, resolve that "I am not the mind, the intellect, nor the vital breath. (16)
The aggregate (saṃghāta) is likewise not "I," being distinct in character from the visible;
therefore, carefully determine the seer through inference. 17.
Understand that "I" am he by whose mere presence entities such as the body and the senses become capable of activities like abandoning and so forth. 18.
Understand that which, remaining free from modification, moves the intellect and other faculties like a magnet, as the directly perceived "I. 19.
Determine that "I am He," by whose presence even the insentient body, senses, mind, and vital breath appear as if they possess a sentient self. 20.
"My mind went elsewhere, and now it has been made steady;
know that I am he who understands the movement of the intellect in this way. (21)
He who directly knows, without undergoing change, the dreaming and waking states, as well as the existence and non-existence of mental states—he, understand him, is "I. 22.
Just as a lamp that illuminates a jar is held to be distinct from the jar, so too am I, the embodied soul whose form is consciousness, distinct from the body that I illuminate. (23)
Determine this: I am that very one who is the most beloved of all, for whom states such as sons, wealth, and the like are dear only insofar as they are subordinate to me.
"May I never cease to exist as the object of the supreme love of others;
may I always be thus"—he who perceives in this way, know him to be "I. 25.
That awakening characterized as the witness is called the meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha).
Furthermore, this witnesshood of the Self consists in its being the cognizer by virtue of its changelessness. (26)
Distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and ego,
you are designated by the term "Thou" (tvaṃpada), having completely abandoned all six kinds of modifications of being.
Having thus ascertained the nature of the object, one should further contemplate that object both by way of exclusion of what it is not (atadvyāvṛtti) and directly through affirmation (vidhimukha).
With all the defects of transmigratory existence cast away, characterized by "not gross" and so forth,
possessing qualities such as invisibility and the like, it is devoid of the impurity of darkness.

He whose bliss is unsurpassed, who is the Truth, whose form is pure consciousness, whose specific characteristic is existence, and who is complete—He is celebrated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 30 ||
Understand that he whose omniscience, supreme lordship, and likewise his perfect power are established by the Vedas is Brahman. 31.
Understand that through the knowledge of which all things are known—as set forth in the Vedas by means of various illustrations such as clay and the like—that is Brahman. 32.
Since the Śruti, having asserted infinity, proclaimed the world's being an effect of that [Brahman] for its establishment, understand that it refers to Brahman. 33.
That which is sought with great effort by those desiring liberation in the Vedāntas for the sake of being known—determine that to be Brahman. 34.
That whose entry into beings as the individual soul (jīvātman) and its governance over them are heard of in the Vedas—know that to be Brahman. 35.
Determine that the Brāhmaṇa is that very one whose role as the bestower of the fruits of actions is heard in the Śruti, while for living beings, he is merely the instrumental agent. || 36 ||
The meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* have been determined; now the meaning of the sentence is considered.
Here, the meaning of the sentence is the identity (*tādātmya*) of those very two word-meanings. (37)
Neither a relational connection (*saṃsarga*) nor a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is accepted here as the meaning of the sentence;
rather, the meaning of the sentence is held by the wise to be an indivisible, single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*). 38.
That which shines as inward consciousness is characterized by non-dual bliss;
and that which is of the nature of non-dual bliss is characterized solely by inward consciousness. (39)
When there occurs such a realization of mutual identity, at that very moment, the non-Brahminhood of the referent "thou" (tvam-artha) is indeed eliminated. (40)
And if the object of that [knowledge] is indeed remote, hear what follows from this:
the inner consciousness abides as the singular form of perfect bliss. (41)

And the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others function by taking up both the referents of the words "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam) as their two intended objects (lakṣya) for the purpose of establishing identity. 42.
Setting aside the two [types of] variegated speech, the sentence is to be discussed for the sake of awakening the meaning of the sentence;
we have explained it with care in the manner in which it functions for us. 43.
That consciousness which, being inseparable from the internal organ, appears as the objective referent of our notions and words—that is what is denoted by the term "thou" (tvaṃpada). 44.

The source of the world, characterized by omniscience and other such qualities, having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), variegated by remoteness, and consisting of reality (*satya*) and the rest, is denoted by the word "That" (*tat-pada*). || 45 ||

Since the simultaneous presence of being perceptible and imperceptible, as well as being accompanied by a second and yet being complete, is contradictory for a single entity, therefore figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is employed. 46.

But when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge and the primary meaning cannot be accepted, the cognition of that which is invariably concomitant with the primary meaning is called indication (lakṣaṇā). || 47 ||
In sentences such as "That thou art," the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is one of partial indication (bhāga-lakṣaṇā);
it is not anything other than that found in the words of a sentence such as "This is that. 48.
Until the understanding of the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman" becomes firm, one should practice hearing and the other means of inquiry, accompanied by tranquility and the other virtues. (49)
When, through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, firm realization arises, then the person has cast off the entire cause of saṃsāra. 50.
With his organs of action and perception dissolved, unenveloped by the subtle elements,
and freed from the fetters of karma, he is liberated immediately.
When one becomes liberated while living by the force of prārabdha karma, after a short time, upon the exhaustion of the bondage of uncommenced (anārabdha) karma; || 52 ||
He attains the supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is an unsurpassed bliss, free from rebirth, and absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 53 ||
Thus ends the Vākyavṛtti, the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
